key_developments.event: Aghlabid invasion of Sicily begins — Islamic-Christian Mediterranean coexistence intensifies.
Venice obtains chrysobull from Alexios I — duty-free trade in Byzantine empire.
Fourth Crusade hands Venice control of the Aegean.
Florence introduces the gold florin — first stable European gold coinage in 600 years.
Genoa's gold genovino debuts; Venice's ducat (1284) follows.
Bardi and Peruzzi (Florence) collapse — first major medieval banking crisis.
Fall of Constantinople severs Venetian access to Black Sea.

_quarry.description: The maritime commercial system that knit Christian and Islamic Mediterranean shorelines into a single shared economy. From the late 9th century, Italian maritime republics (Amalfi, Venice, Pisa, Genoa) developed the colleganza partnership, double-entry bookkeeping, and the bill of exchange — financial instruments that decoupled commerce from physical bullion shipment. The Crusades opened the Levantine coast to Italian merchant colonies. By 1300 a Genoese or Venetian merchant could sit in Florence and direct cargo from Alexandria via Trebizond, Famagusta, and Bruges. The system gave Europe the capital surplus that financed early-modern overseas expansion.
